title: RAG in Python: splitters, fusion and retrieval metrics
seriesDescription: Python and FastAPI interview topics in JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short Python/SQL code and multi-correct questions. Python only: nothing here mixes in Java.
description: Python code for RAG: text splitters, reciprocal rank fusion, recall@k, MRR and nDCG functions, cosine similarity and the arithmetic of chunks and vectors.
source: langchain-text-splitters 1.1 and NumPy run locally; Cormack et al. RRF paper (SIGIR 2009); Manning, Raghavan, Schutze: Introduction to Information Retrieval

questions.prompt: Using LangChain, write Python that creates a RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_size 800, chunk_overlap 100 and the separators paragraph break, newline, space, then empty string (in that order).

checks.label: lists separators from paragraph down to empty string

questions.model:
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=800,
    chunk_overlap=100,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", " ", ""],
)
chunks = splitter.split_text(text)
questions.explanation: By default the size is measured in characters (len), not tokens; use from_tiktoken_encoder to count tokens. chunk_overlap must be smaller than chunk_size or the splitter raises a ValueError. The separators list is also the default order.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function rrf(rankings, k=60) where rankings is a list of ranked lists of document ids (best first). Return the document ids sorted by fused RRF score, highest first.
questions.explanation: Other solutions pass (defaultdict, 0-based enumerate with k + rank + 1). Ties are broken arbitrarily unless you add a secondary key.

questions.prompt: Write two Python functions: recall_at_k(retrieved, relevant, k) returning the fraction of the relevant ids found in the first k retrieved ids, and mrr(runs) where runs is a list of (retrieved, relevant) pairs, returning the mean reciprocal rank of the first relevant hit (0 for a miss).

checks.label: divides by the number of relevant docs

questions.explanation: Other layouts pass (a generator with next(), 0-based enumerate with rank + 1). Guard against an empty relevant set in real code.

questions.prompt: Write a Python function ndcg_at_k(rels, k) where rels is the list of graded relevance scores of the retrieved documents in rank order. Use DCG = sum of rel / log2(position + 1) over the first k results and divide by the DCG of the ideal ordering (the same scores sorted best first).

checks.label: divides DCG by the ideal DCG

questions.explanation: enumerate starts at 0, so the position is i + 1 and log2(position + 1) becomes log2(i + 2). I ran it: ndcg_at_k([1, 0, 1], 3) is 0.9197, the 92 from the earlier integer question. In a real evaluation the ideal list must come from all relevant documents, not only the retrieved ones, and an empty ideal needs the guard shown.

questions.prompt: With NumPy imported as np, write cosine(a, b) for two equal-length lists of numbers: the dot product divided by the product of the two vector norms, returned as a float.
questions.explanation: I checked cosine([3, 4], [4, 3]) = 0.96. If both vectors are already L2-normalised the norms are 1 and the dot product alone is the cosine, which is why many vector stores use a dot-product index. A zero vector would divide by zero, so guard it in real code.

questions.prompt: A string text has 2,100 characters. How many chunks does [text[i:i + 500] for i in range(0, len(text), 400)] produce?
questions.explanation: range(0, 2100, 400) yields starts 0, 400, 800, 1200, 1600 and 2000, so there are 6 chunks. The last one holds only 100 characters, all of them already inside the previous chunk's overlap. I ran it; with a 2,000-character text the same code gives 5, so the last start can add a chunk that carries no new text.

questions.prompt: np.zeros((1000, 1536), dtype=np.float32).nbytes holds 1,000 embeddings of 1,536 dimensions. What number of bytes does it report?
questions.explanation: 1,000 x 1,536 x 4 bytes (float32) = 6,144,000 bytes, about 6.1 MB, which I confirmed by running it. A million vectors is 1,000 times that, roughly 6.1 GB before any index overhead.

questions.prompt: A teammate's reciprocal rank fusion ends with return sorted(scores, key=scores.get) and the worst documents come back first. What is the bug?

options.text: sorted sorts ascending by default, so reverse=True is missing.
options.why: Right: the key function is fine, but the default ascending order puts the lowest fused score first.

options.text: scores.get is not allowed as a sort key, so the dictionary must be converted to a list.
options.why: dict.get works as a key function and returns each document's score.

options.text: The score should be multiplied by the rank, so higher ranks sort to the end of the list.
options.why: RRF adds 1 / (k + rank) per list; multiplying by the rank would reverse the intent.

options.text: sorted returns the scores themselves instead of the document ids in this call.
options.why: Iterating a dict yields its keys, so the call returns document ids as intended.

questions.explanation: sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True) is the fix. A quick unit test with two tiny rankings catches this kind of ordering bug immediately.

questions.prompt: Assertion and reason: read both statements and choose the right option.
questions.assertion: For two L2-normalised NumPy vectors a and b, the expression a @ b equals their cosine similarity.
questions.reason: The norm of a normalised vector is 1, so the denominator of the cosine formula is 1.

whys.a: Both true, and R explains A: with both norms equal to 1 the formula cosine = a.b / (|a||b|) reduces to a.b.
whys.b: Not chosen: R is not a side fact; it is exactly why the formula simplifies.
whys.c: Not chosen: R is true, because normalising divides a vector by its length.
whys.d: Not chosen: A is true, so the dot product of unit vectors is the cosine.

questions.explanation: I checked it: [3, 4]/5 dotted with [4, 3]/5 gives 0.96, the same as the cosine of the raw vectors.

questions.text: Call {1} to cut a plain string into a list of strings, {2} to split Document objects while copying their metadata to each chunk, and {3} to turn raw strings plus optional metadata into Document chunks.
